The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
authors: Roza Izmailyan, Mher Matevosyan, Hamlet Khachatryan, Anastasiya Shavina, Smbat Gevorgyan, Artur Ghazaryan, Irina Tirosyan, Yeva Gabrielyan, Marusya Ayvazyan, Boris Martirosyan, Vardan Harutyunyan, Hovakim Zakaryan
abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.
comment: Accepted manuscript. 13 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (supplementary text, Tables S1-S2, Figures S1-S5). Published in Antiviral Research 222 (2024) 105818

title: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Logarithm
authors: Yuwen Zhou
abstract: Is computing a Diffie-Hellman key as hard as computing a discrete logarithm? Maurer showed that it is, given a few bits of advice, provided that short intervals contain enough integers with only small prime factors; that proviso has stood for thirty years. We remove it. For every prime $p$ there is an advice string of $O(\log p)$ bits, depending only on $p$, with which discrete logarithms in every group of order $p$ are computed in polynomial time from a Diffie-Hellman oracle. The reduction is the classical one; what was missing was a proof that short intervals contain polylogarithmically smooth integers. We show that a zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function, which is now known, gives the expected number of $(\log x)^K$-smooth integers in every interval $[x,x+x^θ]$ with $θ>17/30$. With smoothness this small the saddle point of the counting integral lies just to the left of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, and a zero-free strip of any fixed width absorbs the shift once $K$ is large. Genus-2 Jacobians, whose orders fill such intervals, then turn one of these integers into the order of an auxiliary group. The same input removes the smoothness assumption from Maurer and Raub's impossibility of field-homomorphic one-way permutations and from the yes/no-query reduction of Koblitz, Menezes and Shparlinski. It also makes Wolf's characterisation unconditional: discrete logarithm and Diffie-Hellman are generically equivalent exactly when the group order has no large repeated prime factor.
comment: 15 pages. Developed with Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic); see "Use of AI". Companion paper on the hyperelliptic curve method: https://github.com/OctopusTide/hyperelliptic-curve-method

title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
authors: Kareem Hegazy, Eric C-Y Yuan, Anup Kumar, Dmitriy Morozov, Daniel Barter, Michael W Mahoney, Teresa Head-Gordon, Samuel M Blau
abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

title: Multilevel Filtering on Manifolds with Light Schrödinger Bridges
authors: Jason Beh, Pierre Del Moral, Ajay Jasra
abstract: In this article we consider the filtering of partially observed diffusions when the observations, made at discrete times, are noiseless. Each observation then confines the hidden state to a manifold defined by the data, whose type, for instance a sphere or an affine subspace, may change from one observation time to the next. In practice, the filter is approximated by particle filters, which require the diffusion to be discretized in time. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces the cost of this discretization only if the particle approximations at consecutive discretization levels stay close, which standard particle filters do not ensure. We develop a new particle filter based on light Schrödinger bridges, which works between changing manifolds and can be coupled across discretization levels. A key insight is that the previous state enters the light Schrödinger bridge only through a few features, so that the bridge only has to be fitted on the new manifold, regardless of the type of the previous one. We bound the bias of this particle filter and the gap between its approximations at consecutive levels, and show numerically, on spheres and on manifolds that change type, that this gap is much smaller than with standard multilevel particle filters, and that, with the cost of the fits included, a hybrid estimator that uses it at the fine levels reduces the cost at small tolerances.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
authors: Yury Lysogorskiy, Anton Bochkarev, Ralf Drautz
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
authors: W.J. Rutten, L.F.P. Etman, F. Warmer
abstract: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Fusion Engineering and Design

title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $α$-Stable MIMO Channels
authors: Rawad Kansoh, Bahaa Ammoury, Charbel Hannoun, Jihad Fahs, Ibrahim Abou-Faycal
abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $α$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $α$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $α$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.

title: On (Pathwidth, Clique)-boundedness
authors: Amir Nikabadi
abstract: We prove that every $(\pw,ω)$-bounded class of graphs has bounded tree-independence number, answering a question of Bešter Štorgel, Dallard, Lozin, Milanič, and Zamaraev. We deduce this from a bound on the tree-independence number of graphs with neither $\B_ρ$ nor $K_{σ,σ}$ as an induced minor, where $\B_ρ$ is the complete binary tree of height $ρ$ and the bound depends only on $ρ$ and $σ$. We then obtain an asymptotically sharp bound on the path-independence number of $n$-vertex graphs in any $(\pw,ω)$-bounded class. The lower-bound examples also give counterexamples to a conjecture of Hickingbotham and Joret. We further prove that, for every forest $F$ and every $\ell\in\N$, there is a constant $k=k(F,\ell)\in\N$ such that every graph $G$ with no induced theta or $\ell$-long prism and no induced subgraph isomorphic to $F$ satisfies tree-independence number at most $k$. This proves a strengthened form of a conjecture of Chudnovsky, Hajebi, and Trotignon. Finally, for every integer $s\ge2$, we characterize the forests $F$ for which excluding $F$ as an induced minor and $K_{s,s}$ as an induced subgraph bounds tree-independence number. This extends the characterization of Bonnet, Duhamel, and Hickingbotham, who considered bounded pathwidth with $K_{s,s}$ excluded as a subgraph.

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
authors: Sergei Iudin, Mikhail Podobrii, Dmitry Zheltkov, Stanislav Moiseev
abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.
comment: 39 pages, including supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/antientropic-guy/OhMyU1_public. Extends an earlier version presented at the non-archival CoLoRAI workshop at ICML 2026

title: Critical heavy traffic and diffusion limits for shortest-of-d dynamic routing
authors: Elmira Yu. Kalimulina
abstract: We study shortest-of-$d$ routing, with fixed $d\ge2$, in $N$ parallel queues with independent finite-state Markov service environments switching at rate $κ_N$. At the critical load $ρ_N=1-1/N$, the empirical measure of the centered queue lengths, under stationarity, converges in distribution to a random probability measure determined by its mean. We identify the mean's density and the conditional independence of fixed finite collections of centered queues in the limit. On time scales of order $N$, the centered empirical mean converges to a diffusion with explicit drift and constant diffusion coefficient. These limits hold when $κ_N/N\to\infty$, along subsequences with convergent lattice phase. The diffusion limit extends to centered initial empirical measures tight in the first Wasserstein topology, with means converging in law. A short initial layer prepares the limiting family while preserving the limiting mean. Empirical approximation holds in time-integrated Wasserstein distance.

title: FAST: Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing for Quickest Change Detection
authors: Peiyao Liu, Jie Guo, Zhijun Wang, Xueru Zhang, Nan Chen
abstract: Quickest change detection (QCD) is studied for partially observed functional data streams. At each sampling epoch, a function is realized over a continuous domain, but its values can be observed at only a fixed number of locations. At an unknown change point, the functional mean undergoes a shift that is assumed to admit a sparse representation in a localized basis. We propose Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing (FAST), which jointly estimates the unknown post-change parameter, selects sensing locations, and performs sequential detection. A minimax lower bound on the worst-case detection delay is derived under an average-run-length constraint. A non-asymptotic estimation-error bound is established for the policy-dependent observations induced by adaptive sensing. Under the stated regularity conditions, FAST is first-order asymptotically optimal when sensing subsets are optimized exactly. Simulations and a wildfire case study demonstrate the performance of the proposed procedure.

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
authors: Davi Castro-Silva, Ryan Dancy, Sergii Strelchuk
abstract:
Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each).
  Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement.
  By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
authors: Daniel Maroto Sanchez, Christian Velasco-Gallego, Miriam Bastante Chichon, Jaime Álvarez-Benayas, Tsoulakos Nikolaos, J. A. Bravo-Montes
abstract: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.

title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
authors: Artem Guba, Nikolay Kovalev, Alexey Zharinov, Vacheslav Demin, Viktor B. Kazantsev
abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
authors: Ons Zammel, Carlos Soares, Flávia Carvalhido, Gerd Kortemeyer
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
authors: Kunqi Huang, Lican Kang, Hongrui Shu, Jincheng Ying
abstract: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

title: Transmission Expansion and Energy Storage Planning under Great Britain's Uncertain Energy Transition Pathways
authors: Shengming Cao, Runsheng He, Waqquas Bukhsh
abstract: Long term power system planning must account for uncertainty in electricity demand and generation, while recognising the different investment and commissioning characteristics of transmission and energy storage. This paper develops a multi year stochastic framework for coordinated transmission expansion and energy storage planning and applies it to the Great Britain electricity system to assess investment needs through to 2050. The framework integrates multiple energy transition pathways with an enhanced representation of the GB transmission network and captures the different characteristics of transmission and storage investment over time. The coordinated treatment of transmission and storage is considered as a system level benchmark rather than a centralised investment mechanism. In GB, transmission investment is subject to regulated forward looking planning, while storage is largely developed by market participants in response to market signals. The framework therefore quantifies the potential value of improved coordination and identifies where existing investment signals may not encourage complementary storage deployment. Results across alternative transmission only, storage only and coordinated investment strategies show substantial benefits from joint planning. Compared with transmission only planning, coordinated investment reduces additional transmission capacity by 2%, cumulative expected load shedding by 97%, and total expected system cost by 36%, primarily through avoided unserved energy. Transmission preparation periods affect the timing, but not the final portfolio, of investments. Finally, the energy transition pathway materially influences investment requirements, with Electrification and Efficiency requiring 7% more transmission capacity and 45% more storage energy capacity than Falling Behind.

title: Sharp lower bounds for weighted bisections of graphs with bounded maximum degree
authors: Stefanie Gerke, Gregory Gutin, Anders Yeo, Yacong Zhou
abstract: A bisection of a graph is a partition of its vertex set into two parts the sizes of which differ by at most one. We prove that every finite simple graph of maximum degree at most an odd positive integer $k$, with arbitrary nonnegative real edge weights, has a bisection of weight at least $(k+1)/(2k)$ times its total edge weight. The corresponding bound $(k+2)/(2(k+1))$ for even $k$ follows immediately. Both coefficients are best possible. Somewhat surprisingly, these are exactly the sharp coefficients known for maximum weighted cuts, despite the additional balance requirement.

title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
authors: Marc Braun, Adel Daoud, Jose M. Peña
abstract: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows
authors: Zengyuan Zuo, Junjun Jiang, Fei Mu, Xubo Wang, Xianming Liu
abstract: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

title: Heap-type permutation generation with a prescribed final arrangement
authors: Luís M. S. Russo
abstract: Heap's algorithm generates all permutations of an array of n items, obtaining each one from its predecessor by a single swap. We determine the net permutation applied to the array by every complete recursive call: a transposition when the number of items is odd and at least three, and a cycle through all items when it is even. We show that the output of each call is a concatenation of right cosets of the symmetric group on one item fewer, and we prove a general formula: the order in which the items are parked at the last position may be chosen freely, every such order corresponds to exactly one valid schedule, and it determines the net permutation of the call. Two variants follow. In the cyclic variant a complete sweep over an even number of items rotates the array by one position. In the extremal variant, for even n, a sweep started from the identity ends in the lexicographically largest arrangement that any single-swap enumeration can leave; by a parity argument this is the reversal exactly when n is congruent to 2 modulo 4. The construction of the extremal variant is proved correct when n is divisible by 4 and verified by computer for all even n up to 10000.

title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
authors: Evgeny Alves Limarenko
abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
authors: Y.-H. Taguchi
abstract:
For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $Δ= [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not.
  We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $π$ to $π\circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $Δ(π) = -Δ(π\circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in.
  The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $σ$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.
comment: 41 pages. Ancillary files contain the measurement and verification scripts. Prepared with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude for drafting, revision and the verification scripts; OpenAI ChatGPT for a critical reading of a draft); all measurements were produced and verified by the author, who is responsible for the content

title: First Order Geometry of Equilateral Small Polygons
authors: José Ayala Hoffmann, Tomás Ayala Coppola
abstract:
We develop a first order calculus based on the geometry of realised diameter graphs for perimeter maximisation among convex equilateral small polygons. Polygon side equalities and active diameter constraints define a linearised feasible cone and an associated equality space. We prove that an equilateral small polygon is a strict local maximiser of perimeter modulo Euclidean motions if a multiplier balance holds with strictly positive active diameter multipliers and the active equality space consists only of infinitesimal Euclidean motions. The proof uses a local Euclidean slice and a geometric limiting argument and requires neither independence of the active constraint gradients nor second order information.
  As an application, we combine our criterion with validated interval arithmetic to establish strict local maximality for Bingane and Audet's polygons $A_{16}$, $A_{32}$, $A_{64}$ and for reconstructions of their polygons $Z_{32}$ and $Z_{64}$. For each $n\in\{32,64\}$, the perimeter of $Z_n$ is strictly larger than that of $A_n$. Thus, strict local maximisers with different perimeters coexist in the space of convex equilateral small polygons with the same number of sides.

title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
authors: Hoang-Viet Nguyen, Hai-Dang Dau, Alexandre H. Thiéry
abstract: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

title: Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
authors: Oded Levi, Boaz Rafaely
abstract: First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index ($C_{50}$), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

title: StreamingDPD: A 1.28-GSa/s Instantaneous-Power-Gated Depthwise TCN Accelerator for Real-Time 320-MHz Digital Predistortion
authors: Yizhuo Wu, Xinling Wang, Chang Gao
abstract: State feedback between successive samples limits the streaming throughput of recurrent neural networks for digital predistortion (DPD). We present StreamingDPD, an accelerator that processes 320-MHz signals at 1.28 GSa/s. Its 207-parameter instantaneous-power-gated depthwise temporal convolutional network (IPG-DWTCN) uses $|x[n]|^2$ to gate feature channels and causal dilated depthwise convolutions to model power amplifier memory. The network maps to a spatially unrolled fixed-point pipeline with shift-based quadratic activations and layer-wise mixed precision, sustaining one complex sample per cycle per lane. Its algorithmic cost is 554 floating-point operations per complex sample, 30.1% fewer than the recurrent baseline with the best linearization performance. In RF playback measurements on three power amplifiers driven by 40- to 320-MHz Wi-Fi 6/7 and 5G NR waveforms, IPG-DWTCN achieves the lowest mean adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR) and ranks first or ties for first in mean error vector magnitude (EVM) against five neural baselines of comparable size. Four-lane FPGA hardware-in-the-loop tests on a 320-MHz 4096-QAM Wi-Fi 7 waveform achieve -45.82 dBc ACPR and -42.94 dB EVM at 1.28 GSa/s. At the same sample rate, post-layout evaluation of a single-lane 12-nm FinFET ASIC yields a 0.10 mm$^2$ core, a 52-cycle (40.63 ns) latency, and an estimated typical-corner power of 142.21 mW (111.10 pJ/sample). Relative to the prior 22-nm recurrent DPD ASIC, the design provides 5.1 times the throughput at about one-seventh the energy per sample.

title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
authors: Chariton Chalvatzis
abstract: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

title: Inference after coding agents
authors: Florian Gunsilius, David Van Dijcke, Kaspar Wüthrich
abstract: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
authors: Vladimir A. Lazovskiy, Victor B. Kazantsev, Sergey V. Stasenko
abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
authors: Thomas Huffstutler
abstract: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
authors: Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
authors: Zhaosong Lu, Yifeng Xiao
abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
comment: Accepted by SIAM Journal on Optimization

title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
authors: Xingyang Yu
abstract: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper to an 18-volume textbook collection. Textbook PDFs: https://xingyangyu.com/textbook/

title: Nanorobot queue: Cooperative treatment of cancer based on team member communication and image processing
authors: Xinyu Zhou
abstract: Although nanorobots have been used as clinical prescriptions for work such as gastroscopy, and even photoacoustic tomography technology has been proposed to control nanorobots to deliver drugs at designated delivery points in real time, and there are cases of eliminating "superbacteria" in blood through nanorobots, most technologies are immature, either with low efficiency or low accuracy, Either it can not be mass produced, so the most effective way to treat cancer diseases at this stage is through chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Patients are suffering and can not be cured. Therefore, this paper proposes an ideal model of a treatment method that can completely cure cancer, a cooperative treatment method based on nano robot queue through team member communication and computer vision image classification (target detection).
