One- and two-dimensional numerical tests with multiplicative noise validate the predicted convergence rates and compare the computational performance of explicit stabilized methods against the linearly implicit Euler method.

title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
authors: Kaixiang Wang, Junjie Li, Zhaojiacheng Zhou, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
abstract: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

title: Data Center Governance Under AI Expansion Pressures
authors: Yacine Jernite, Sasha Luccioni, Bruna Trevelin, Angela Lee, Carolina Molina, Xinying Chu
abstract: The promised benefits of data centers are global, but their negative impacts are very much local, affecting the energy bills, aquifers and living environments of citizens across the United States. While governments and authorities have historically provided data centers with incentives such as tax credits and exemptions, AI's aggressive growth in scale has changed this dynamic, and recent months have seen them issue bills and file lawsuits in order to ensure that data centers remain a net positive influence on their legislatures. Existing pieces of federal legislation -- such as the Public Trust Doctrine, the Pollution Prevention, Clean Air and Safe Drinking Water Acts -- exist to manage natural resources, but their scope remains contested, and the current federal government's stance on competitiveness and growth of AI has put the onus on regional governments to endeavor to protect local resources. There are also state- and regional laws and regulations that are relevant for building and operating data centers since, in practice, they require substantial land, electricity, water, and infrastructure at a local level. Given this situation, communities are currently provided with the opportunity to raise their concerns regarding the potential negative impacts of how data centers are built and operated, and have existing regulations that can be used to put pressure on data center operators.

title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
authors: Carson Dudley, Reiden Magdaleno, Yutong Bi, Anthony Valencia, Xiaofeng Liu, Marisa Eisenberg
abstract:
Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data.
  Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence.
  Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

title: SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting
authors: Amir Rafe, Iman Jamshidi, Gourab Sil, Subasish Das
abstract: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.

title: Survivability Guarantees for Delayed Serial Supply Chains under Demand Shocks
authors: Lorenzo Giordano, Francesco Lo Iudice, Josep M. Olm, Marco Coraggio
abstract: When demand exceeds the maximum production capacity of a supply chain, it can be satisfied only for a finite time, determined by the inventory stored along the chain. Existing control methods ensure indefinite constraint satisfaction under bounded demand, but provide no guarantees on how long a supply chain can withstand a shock in which demand goes beyond production capacity. We address this gap for a serial supply chain with transportation delays and flow constraints. Under a specified flow policy, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the inventory distribution that guarantee a prescribed lower bound on the exit time from the set where demand is served. We use these conditions to compute inventory targets that minimize holding costs via a quadratic program. Then, we propose a two-mode controller that builds reserves under ordinary demand and depletes them during the shock. Simulations illustrate this approach.

title: A Modulation Strategy for Bidirectional Integrated Onboard and Wireless EV Charging
authors: Manveer Aujla, Gavin Feher, Caniggia Viana
abstract: Integrated electric vehicle chargers reduce cost by sharing power conversion hardware between the onboard charger (OBC) and the wireless charger (WC). A previously proposed dual active bridge (DAB)-based OBC/WC shares the rectification stage between the OBC and WC; however, the modulation required to realize its wireless operation has not yet been reported. This paper details a modulation strategy that enables the operation of the integrated OBC/WC topology. Differential-mode operation is used for the OBC, and common-mode operation is used for the WC. In OBC mode, the shared full-bridge produces differential-mode voltage for wired power transfer while ideally generating zero common-mode voltage on the wireless charging path. In WC mode, the same full-bridge produces common-mode voltage for wireless power transfer while ideally generating zero differential-mode voltage on the onboard charging path. The method preserves conventional DAB phase-shift power control and enables bidirectional power transfer in wired and wireless charging modes without additional contactors. Design considerations for the OBC transformer and WC coils are derived based on the resulting square-wave voltage amplitudes. Offline PLECS simulations demonstrate power tracking and decoupled charger operation at $\pm$7.4 kW. Hardware-in-the-loop simulations using a PLECS RT Box and an external Texas Instruments microcontroller further validate the proposed modulation method.
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures. Accepted version of a paper presented at the 2026 IEEE Energy Conversion Congress and Expo (ECCE), Vancouver, Canada

title: A Disease-specific Retinal Aging Biomarker for Predicting Progression to Late Age-related Macular Degeneration
authors: Hexin Dong, Benjamin Hou, Puzhen Wu, Mingquan Lin, Emily Y. Chew, Zhiyong Lu, Yifan Peng
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults. While chronological age is a primary risk factor, it inadequately reflects individual variations in retinal aging, limiting effective AMD risk stratification and timely intervention. Here, we propose and validate fundus-based AMD age (FAA), which quantifies disease-specific retinal aging in AMD and captures accelerated AMD-related retinal aging, thereby improving prognostic precision over chronological age. Trained on 36,782 images from 2,192 participants in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) dataset and validated across AREDS and AREDS2 cohorts, our model demonstrates significant improvements over traditional chronological age-based approaches. Specifically, integrating the proposed FAA into Cox proportional-hazards models significantly enhances prediction performance. FAA improved the C-index from 0.836 to 0.888 and reduced the 5-year Brier score from 0.050 to 0.046 in AREDS, with consistent gains observed in AREDS2 (C-index 0.715 to 0.756; 2-year Brier 0.078 to 0.076). FAA showed improved prognostic performance across the two datasets and under different phenotype definitions (reading center-defined vs. specialist-defined grading), supporting its potential utility for AMD risk stratification. These findings highlight the advantage of incorporating FAA into AMD risk prediction frameworks, supporting further evaluation of FAA for AMD risk stratification.

title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
authors: Translated, Maria Pia Adinolfi, Isabelle Andrieu, Grazia Fiorella Anfuso, Melania Annunziata, Daniele Antonini, Marta Arena, Luca Barone, Dana Barras Franco, Francesca Basiricò, Francesca Bee, Sofia Bertini, Nicola Bertoldi, Giorgio Biancini, Alessandra Bigi, Giulia Boccalini, Tommaso Bonomo, Enrico Boscardi, Sebastien Bratieres, Francesco Brigante, Giulia Brignola, Romolo Buondestino, Brenda Patricia Byrne, Giorgia Campora, Edoardo Cappelli, Veronica Carascosi, Francesca Carducci, Cody Carlson, Davide Caroselli, Ambra Cascio, Dario Cascio, Mauro Cassani, Andrea Castro, Alessandro Cattelan, Giulia Ceccacci, Paola Cellini, Giulia Chiriatti, Federico Cialini, Valentina Ciarlariello, Daniele Cocozza, Emanuela Coghe, Kathleen Compares, Marco Comunità, Davide Conti, Helen Rebecca Corfield, Michele Cortellessa, Anna Cracco, Aurora Cuppone, Arianna D'Andrea, Maurizio Davoli, Andrea De Angelis, Andrea De Blasi, Rebecca De Giorgi, Annalisa De Petra, Arianna De Pilla, Joris Demiraj, Elena Deufemia, Federica Di Antonio, Pierluigi Di Cianni, Vincenzo Di Cicco, Michela Di Clemente, Alan Di Francesco, Ylenia Di Gese, Federica Di Iulio, Claudia Di Lorenzo, Andrea Di Paola, Giulia Di Pilla, Jessica Dickson, Francesco Elefante, Ilaria Fabrizio, Alessandro Falappa, Viviana Fantozzi, Antonio Farina, Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro.Diego Andrea, Andrea Ferrari, Sara Ferri, Simona Ferri, Fabio Fioramonti, Stefano Florio, Mariachiara Fornaro, Anna Maria Foti, Niccolò Fransoni, Alessandro Fusacchia, Emma Gamba, Francesco Gasperoni, Davide Gattini, Marta Giani, Claudia Giannetti, Valerio Giannini, Antonella Giudici, Mara Gramendola, Michele Grandinetti, Eleonora Graziani, L'Meese Hope Greaney, Dario Gubernari, Filomena Guglielmi, Jonathan Hammond, Stephen William Harris, Rowena Elizabeth Hogg, Marta Hontanon Del Olmo
abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

title: An algorithm for solving the Burgers equation based on rational approximations and the collocation method
authors: I.A. Bugoets, B.V. Semisalov
abstract: We propose a numerical method for solving initial-boundary value problems for the Burgers equation that takes into account the presence of singularities of the analytic continuation of the solution into the complex plane. The algorithm uses rational approximations, a collocation method and a new scheme for time discretization combined with the relaxation method. An adaptive strategy is developed to account for the location of the singular point of the solution. Solutions to the well-known benchmark problem with a sine-shaped initial condition are obtained for the values of the viscosity as low as nu = 10^-8. Verification of the numerical results in such an extreme parameter regime makes it necessary to modify a classical formula for the exact solution so as to avoid floating-point overflow during its computation. The developed method is compared with an algorithm employing the Runge-Kutta scheme, and the conditions under which each approach yields superior results are outlined. An important feature of the proposed method is its capability to track the singular point of the solution. To verify this, we consider a problem whose solution has a simple analytical form and demonstrate that the exact and approximate coordinates of the singular point of the solution agree with high accuracy, even when the singularity comes extremely close to the domain of the problem. Taking the location of the singular point into account yields significant gains in both accuracy and run time relative to other methods.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
authors: Zhengxu Yu, Ke Xu, Meng Fang, Haitham Ammar, Weilin Luo, Jun Wang
abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

title: A binomial-adjusted $θ$-trapezoidal tau-leaping method for chemical kinetic systems
authors: Maximilian Scott, Sam McCallum, James Foster
abstract: In Hu, Li and Min (2011), the authors propose a weak second order accurate $θ$-trapezoidal method as an improvement to the classical tau-leaping method. However, for complex chemical kinetic systems their model's underlying analytical assumptions can fail to hold in practice, leading to a significant reduction in its computational effectiveness. Here we introduce a modification to the method which allows it to regain desirable convergence characteristics, both given the original and a relaxed version of the underlying assumptions. We confirm this improvement through a local error analysis and present numerical examples showing it consistently performs either better or comparable to the $θ$-trapezoidal method.

title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry
authors: Nichula Wasalathilaka, Kevin Dawson, Chinthaka Jacob, Mervyn Parakrama Ekanayake, Roshan Godaliyadda
abstract: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

title: Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech
authors: Mohamed Zakaria Kurdi
abstract:
Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests.
  Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT

title: A PTAS for Constraint Satisfaction Problems on Interval Graphs and Bounded Rank-Width Graphs
authors: Ian DeHaan, Euiwoong Lee
abstract:
We present a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for all Boolean arity-two maximum constraint satisfaction problems (Boolean Max-2-CSP) where the constraint graph is either interval or has bounded rank-width. This class of problems includes, for example, Max-Cut, Max-DiCut, Max-2-Lin(2), and Max-2-SAT. In particular, this settles the approximability of Max-Cut on interval graphs. To achieve these results, we show the following.
  1. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an $n^{\mathcal O(r \varepsilon^{-2})}$-time $(1 - \varepsilon$)-approximation for Boolean Max-2-CSP on graphs of rank-width at most $r$.
  2. There is a polynomial-time algorithm that, for any interval graph $G = (V, E)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, finds a subgraph $H = (V, F)$ of $G$ such that $|F| \geq (1 - \varepsilon) |E|$ and $H$ has rank-width at most $\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon^{-1})$.
  Our techniques additionally extend to all bounded-alphabet arity-two max CSPs.

title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
authors: Jens Lehmann
abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
authors: Ulysse Mizrahi, Sean Zaretzky, Dov Danon, Amit H. Bermano
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
authors: Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Ben Przystanski, LJ Ciccarelli, Natalie Bach, Laura Zarrow
abstract: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
authors: NovaSilicon Team
abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
authors: Shajnin Haque Aishy, Sabbir Bin Abdul Latif, Md. Golam Zel A Husna, Jannatun Noor
abstract: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.

title: Maturity$^2$: Assessing the Maturity of Crypto Agility Maturity Models
authors: Leonie Wolf, Robin Leander Schröder, Sebastian Schinzel, Fabian Ising
abstract: Crypto agility maturity models aim to support organizations in preparing for cryptographic transitions, such as migrating to post-quantum cryptography. Recognizing the importance of measurable maturity, NIST references several such models in its guidance. Given NIST's influence on cybersecurity practice, these models may shape organizational planning and governance mechanisms. However, their design quality has not been systematically evaluated. In this work, we assess three industry-driven maturity models against established design principles. Our analysis reveals recurring weaknesses, particularly the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance for improving crypto agility. At the same time, we highlight individual strengths that can assist practitioners in choosing among the models and derive concrete recommendations for strengthening future crypto agility maturity models.
comment: 19th International Symposium on Foundations & Practice of Security (FPS - 2026)

title: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control
authors: Maarten De Baecke, Flavia Sofia Acerbo, Andrea Giusti, Wilm Decré
abstract: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) \emph{self-informed sampling (SIFS)}, a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4~Hz to 1~kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
authors: Qijia Zhuang, Yanyi Gou, Wenbin Ma, Yuxiang Ren
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps.
  We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively.
  We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA
authors: David Sánchez, Benet Manzanares, Josep Domingo-Ferrer
abstract: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.

title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
authors: Davide Wiest
abstract: Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.

title: Exploring Socially Acceptable 3D Feedback Design for Inclusive Small-Group Conversation
authors: Qianjie Wei, Yifan Li, Zhen Bai
abstract: Prior research has shown that providing feedback on group dynamics can improve the quality of small-group conversations. However, publicly delivered feedback that targets specific individuals may reduce social acceptability due to negative experiences such as social pressure, embarrassment, and resistance. This work investigates how public feedback can be designed to remain socially acceptable while maintaining its effectiveness in XR-based small-group conversations. Informed by social science and HCI literature, we identified three design strategies (incorporate humor, reduce social attention, and use indirectness) and proposed a set of metaphor- and agent-based 3D feedback probes. We then conducted a two-phase study: (1) an online survey with 50 participants to examine how such feedback designs are perceived under public and private delivery, and (2) follow-up interviews with 14 participants who completed the survey to better understand their interpretations and elicit additional insights. Results show that metaphor- and agent-based feedback can reduce social discomfort while maintaining effectiveness. Interview findings further highlighted the role of three strategies in making feedback easier to accept, while requiring careful balance. We also discussed design implications for creating socially acceptable 3D feedback to support inclusive small-group conversations in XR.

title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
authors: Kamrul Hasan, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Oleg V. Komogortsev
abstract: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real--synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91--0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.

title: Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models
authors: Daniel Denley, Robert L. Nicol, Mike J. Chantler
abstract: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.

title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
authors: Ekta U. Samani, Christopher G. Atkeson
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.

title: Control-Gibbs Distribution: Sampling for Optimal Control and Diverse Actions
authors: Shengling Shi
abstract: While conventional optimal control selects an optimal input sequence, probabilistic control assigns probability mass over all possible inputs and exploits a distribution of control sequences. Control distributions help enable exploration, capture diverse solutions, and solve deterministic optimal control problems. This work reviews an important probabilistic model for control distributions, the control-Gibbs distribution, i.e., the Gibbs distribution with an optimal control objective as the energy function. We point out its fundamental role in various probabilistic control frameworks, e.g., maximum entropy control, control-as-inference framework, model predictive path integral control, and energy-based models for control. This provides a model-central perspective to unify these probabilistic control frameworks. We also review the associated extensions of dynamic programming for computing closed-loop control distributions. To sample the control-Gibbs distribution, we consider projected Langevin sampling and develop non-asymptotic guarantees. The guarantees show the dual benefits of sampling the control-Gibbs distribution: obtaining diverse control solutions and solving the deterministic optimal control problem. We provide a numerical example where diverse arm trajectories are sampled from a control-Gibbs distribution.

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
authors: Guoan Wang, Feng Liu
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
authors: Yuyang Wu, Yang Liu, Zequn Xie, Junjie Wang, Dan Yang, Zehao Tan, Ding-Chu Zhang, Junming Yang, Yue Shen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu
abstract: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
authors: Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang
abstract: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

title: Robust Control Design for LTI Systems with Sampling-Time Jitter
authors: Dieter Schwarzmann, Jan Lunze
abstract: Sampling-time jitter makes a sampled-data control loop time-varying, so standard LTI robust-control synthesis does not apply directly. This paper reformulates dynamic output feedback design under bounded, unmeasured sample-to-sample jitter as a robust-control problem. The exact zero-order-hold model is decomposed into a nominal time-invariant plant and a memoryless, time-varying uncertainty block with a norm bound representing the sampling-time jitter. As the block is memoryless, the operator small-gain condition for the time varying loop reduces to a standard robustness test with a matrix norm bound. It is shown that the same test also guarantees uniform exponential stability for every admissible jitter sequence. Embedding the decomposition into a generalized plant with performance channels serves two synthesis objectives with standard robust-control tools: Robust stability with optimized nominal performance through structured H-inf synthesis, and robust performance through mu synthesis with constant scalings. A numerical example shows that jitter can destabilize a control loop with a nominal H-inf controller, whereas both robust designs remain stable and the robust-performance design is less sensitive to jitter at the cost of nominal performance.

title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?
authors: Sriom Chakrabarti, Sean Bin Yang, Arijit Khan, Sebastian Link
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization.
  Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge

title: Finding the Farthest in High Dimensions: Dynamic Diameter and Farthest-Neighbor Search
authors: Mohammad Hajiaghayi, Morteza Monemizadeh
abstract:
We give faster algorithms for diameter and farthest-neighbor search in high-dimensional Euclidean space. For every fixed $1<c<\sqrt2$, we maintain an actual factor-$c$ diameter pair under arbitrary point insertions and deletions, with worst-case update time $n^{2/c^2-1}\poly(d,\log n)$ and space $n^{2/c^2}\poly(d,\log n)$, suppressing logarithmic dependence on the execution length and failure probability. Here $n$ bounds the number of active points. The update exponent improves Indyk's algorithm~\cite{indyk} (SODA'03) bound from $1/c^2$ to $2/c^2-1$, while the space exponent improves from $1+1/c^2$ to $2/c^2$. At $c=\sqrt{3/2}$, the update exponent decreases from $2/3$ to $1/3$. A separate construction achieves approximation exactly $\sqrt2$ with update time polynomial in $d$ and $\log n$. All these guarantees hold against adaptive updates, even when every previous random choice is exposed.
  We also improve the time--space tradeoff near linear space. This construction has an always-correct variant with expected amortized update bounds and requires no advance bound on the number of updates. The dynamic structures store a current answer, so reporting its two point identifiers takes constant time.
  The geometric method also gives static diameter algorithms and a farthest-neighbor structure for a fixed set that answers arbitrary adaptive queries. At approximation $\sqrt2-\varepsilon$, the diameter time is $n^{1+O(\varepsilon)}$, and the query time is $n^{O(\varepsilon)+o(1)}$ with near-linear preprocessing and space, up to polynomial input-parameter factors. On binary points, this improves the $n^{O(\sqrtθ)}$ overhead of the algorithm that Andoni, Jiang, and Zharkov~\cite{ajz2026} (STOC'26) for Hamming approximation $2-θ$ to $n^{O(θ)+o(1)}$.

title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
authors: Shuhan Li, Huankang Guan, Xintong Guo, Yang Bo, Yuyang He, Dunyuan Xu, Jingyan Chen, Fang Liu, Tsz Kin Wan, Jinpeng Chen, Zhenqi He, Yuxuan Hu, Wenbo Li, Han Gao, Qijun Li, Long Chen, Hongsheng Li, Rui Liu
abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
authors: Íñigo Zubeldia, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Miles Cranmer
abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.
comment: Accepted for publication in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), Vol. 346, 2026

title: Semiclassical Scaling Laws of Magnus Quantum Algorithms under Harmonic Confinement
authors: Di Fang, Samuel Orellana Mateo
abstract: The simulation of semiclassical Schrödinger dynamics is often hindered by rapid oscillations, where classical numerical methods and quantum simulation algorithms can suffer severe precision loss as the semiclassical parameter $\varepsilon \to 0$. In this work, we uncover a surprising robustness of high-order Magnus quantum algorithms in the semiclassical regime. We establish two important results. First, we extend the theory of Magnus superconvergence from free-particle reference dynamics to a general class of Schrödinger operators whose reference Hamiltonian includes harmonic confinement. Second, and more importantly, we reveal a nontrivial semiclassical scaling law: while the expansion remainder term bound suggests an error prefactor of $O(\varepsilon^{-(p+1)})$ for a $p$th-order method, we prove that the loss is in fact order-independent and collapses to $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ for all $p$. The key analytical mechanism is the exact Egorov transport associated with quadratic flows in semiclassical Weyl quantization, which enables a symbol-level analysis of the interaction-picture Hamiltonian and its Magnus commutators. Our results show that high-order Magnus quantum algorithms remain far more robust in the semiclassical regime than naive series remainder term counting would suggest.

title: First Order Convergence of Representative Volume Element with Mixed Boundary Condition
authors: Pingbing Ming, Hao Yu
abstract: We study the cell problem with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary condition to reconstruct the effective matrix for two-dimensional scalar divergence-form equations with bounded measurable, and possibly nonsymmetric coefficients. We prove uniform invertibility of the mean-gradient matrix. Moreover, we derive the first-order error estimate when the medium is periodic.

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
authors: Bowen Wang, Osvaldo Simeone
abstract: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
authors: Hao Li, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Hui En Pang, Kairui Hu, Mingze Sun, Runmao Yao, Xinhao Ji, Xiyuan Zheng, Xuanli Chen, Yalun Dai, Yap Kim Hui, Dingwen Zhang, Yuanyuan Gao, Ziang Cao, Cheng Huang Yean, Jackson Peng, Rui Duan, Yaobo Liu, Zetong Wang, Ziwei Liu
abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

title: NonSense: On the (In)security of FPGA Anti-tamper Sensors
authors: Mehmet Ali Cetin, Fatemeh Khojasteh Dana, Saleh Khalaj Monfared, Nima Seyed Aghazadeh, Maryam Saadat Safa, Shahin Tajik
abstract: FPGAs are widely used in mission-critical systems, where a successful physical attack can have serious consequences. This makes resilience to such attacks a critical security requirement. To defend against active physical attacks, such as glitching attacks, modern FPGAs rely on on-chip sensors that detect these disturbances and trigger responses, such as key zeroization, before a device is compromised. These sensors are deployed as both hard-IP blocks and soft-IP cores, and their trustworthiness is often taken for granted. In this work, we challenge that assumption and argue that the sensors themselves are a fragile and underexplored attack surface. Drawing on recent results, we show that both the detection and response mechanisms of state-of-the-art sensors can be bypassed without invasive tampering. We further argue that sensor reliability is reduced by factors rarely captured in threat models, including the spatial and frequency-dependent behavior of the system's power delivery network, which can steer a fault to a target while sparing nearby sensors; environmental conditions such as temperature, which shift detection thresholds; and long-term aging, which drifts sensor calibration and may open silent detection gaps. Finally, we propose a set of countermeasures that harden detection and response mechanisms against these effects.

title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
authors: Stanley Huang, Anthony Baez, Catherine Yeh, Pat Pataranutaporn
abstract: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.

title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
authors: Xinheng Ding, Seyyed Saeid Cheshmi, Ziyang Zhang, Tairan Chen, Wenya Xie, Yu Hou, Rui Zhang, Zirui Liu
abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.

title: Evaluation of Music Version Retrieval Methods for Setlist Identification in Live Concerts
authors: Andres Ferraro, Albin Correya
abstract: Automatic setlist identification aims to identify the songs performed in live concert recordings by matching noisy and variable-quality audio against a database of reference tracks. This task presents challenges beyond conventional music version identification, including substantial arrangement differences, background noise, and the need to process continuous recordings efficiently at large scale. In this work, we evaluate modern music version retrieval methods for setlist identification using the ASID benchmark, comparing the established Re-MOVE system with CLEWS and NAVE, an internal neural audio version embedding model. Our results show that NAVE and CLEWS substantially outperform Re-MOVE. Notably, NAVE uses 256-dimensional embeddings, compared with 1024 dimensions for CLEWS, providing a four-fold reduction in embedding storage while achieving better retrieval performance. We further evaluate music/non-music gating and find modest improvements in detection and temporal coverage, while qualitative analysis suggests that such preprocessing can improve recognition boundaries beyond what the standard ASID metrics capture. Overall, the results demonstrate that segment-level audio embeddings provide a strong basis for scalable setlist identification and that compact representations can achieve strong accuracy under realistic live-concert conditions at much lower storage and serving cost.

title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
authors: Saleh Ashkboos, Dhruv Desai, Lavinia Ghita
abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.

title: SALT: State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer for Single-Temporal Cross-Dataset Structural Localization in Remote Sensing
authors: Aggelos Psiris, Georgios Angelidis, Giorgos Sfikas, Maria Vakalopoulou, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos
abstract: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/SALT
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Computer Vision for Geospatial Image Analysis (GeoCV), IEEE/CVF WACV 2027

title: List Update with Time Windows and Delays without Batch-Serving
authors: Icey Siyi Ai, Jingwei Li, Clifford Stein
abstract: We study list update with time windows and delays when every request requires a separate access. Unlike batch-serving models, serving several requests to one element still incurs one access per request, and each access may change the list for subsequent requests. For time windows of overlap at most $k\ge2$, our deterministic First-Element Removal algorithm is $(3-2/k)$-competitive, hence $3$-competitive in general. Against an oblivious adversary, a randomized adaptation of BIT is $7/4$-competitive on arbitrary $2$-overlap inputs. More generally, on inputs without self-overlap, it is $\left(13/4-9/[2(k+1)]\right)$-competitive for every $k\ge2$. For delays, we give a deterministic $5$-competitive algorithm and a lower bound of $2+\sqrt3$ for deterministic delay-unaware algorithms. Our analyses extend inversion potentials with per-request credits that reconcile different service times and orders.

title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
authors: Siu Wun Cheung, Youngsoo Choi
abstract: Numerical simulation of transport processes in magnetized plasmas is characterized by extreme anisotropy, where diffusion along magnetic field lines can be many orders of magnitude larger than in the perpendicular direction. This anisotropy leads to thin, steep boundary layers and numerical pollution that standard finite element methods struggle to resolve without prohibitive mesh refinement. In this paper, we introduce the Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method (PU-DDFEM), a data-driven local model reduction approach, for anisotropic diffusion. The method utilizes a bottom-up construction to enable a complete offline-online splitting. We parametrize the local magnetic field and boundary conditions to generate a snapshot space that captures the essential physics of plasma confinement. Dominant modes are extracted via a local spectral problem to identify representative features. These modes are then mapped to the global domain using a partition of unity to form a conforming approximation space.
