On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
comment: 51 pages, 13 figures. Code and run records: https://github.com/unifyai/continual-arc

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
authors: Adi Mashiach
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
authors: Yeyuan Liu
abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code, data and prediction files are included as ancillary files

title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
authors: Megha Srivastava, Michael H. Lim, Allison M. Keys, Pranav Murugan, Nate Gruver
abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.
comment: 32 pages, Agentic AI for Biological Discovery Workshop (NeurIPS 2026)

title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
authors: Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hirotaka Yoneda, Masataka Yoneda
abstract:
We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $Ω(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows:
  1. A new lower bound of $Ω(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms.
  2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms.
  3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.
  For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$.
  We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
authors: Ziang Liu, James J. Kim, Yijia Dai, Jennifer J. Sun
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages. Project page: https://codiscovery.ai/contrastive-discovery/

title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
authors: Alex Shtoff
abstract: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.
comment: Software paper for a library I've been working on for more than a year

title: Data augmentation using generative networks to identify dementia
authors: Bahman Mirheidari, Yilin Pan, Daniel Blackburn, Ronan O'Malley, Traci Walker, Annalena Venneri, Markus Reuber, Heidi Christensen
abstract: Data limitation is one of the most common issues in training machine learning classifiers for medical applications. Due to ethical concerns and data privacy, the number of people that can be recruited to such experiments is generally smaller than the number of participants contributing to non-healthcare datasets. Recent research showed that generative models can be used as an effective approach for data augmentation, which can ultimately help to train more robust classifiers sparse data domains. A number of studies proved that this data augmentation technique works for image and audio data sets. In this paper, we investigate the application of a similar approach to different types of speech and audio-based features extracted from interactions recorded with our automatic dementia detection system. Using two generative models we show how the generated synthesized samples can improve the performance of a DNN based classifier. The variational autoencoder increased the F-score of a four-way classifier distinguishing the typical patient groups seen in memory clinics from 58% to around 74%, a 16% improvement

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
authors: Sheethal Bhat, Bogdan Georgescu, Awais Mansoor, Florin C. Ghesu, Sasa Grbic, Andreas Maier
abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
authors: Emre Kutlusan, Yongmin Li
abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
authors: Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Jiangweizhi Peng, Shiyang Li, Sujay Bhatt, Sihan Zeng, Mingyi Hong
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

title: Differential Diagnosis of Frontotemporal Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease using Generative Adversarial Network
authors: Da Ma, Donghuan Lu, Karteek Popuri, Mirza Faisal Beg
abstract: Frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease are two common forms of dementia and are easily misdiagnosed as each other due to their similar pattern of clinical symptoms. Differentiating between the two dementia types is crucial for determining disease-specific intervention and treatment. Recent development of Deep-learning-based approaches in the field of medical image computing are delivering some of the best performance for many binary classification tasks, although its application in differential diagnosis, such as neuroimage-based differentiation for multiple types of dementia, has not been explored. In this study, a novel framework was proposed by using the Generative Adversarial Network technique to distinguish FTD, AD and normal control subjects, using volumetric features extracted at coarse-to-fine structural scales from Magnetic Resonance Imaging scans. Experiments of 10-folds cross-validation on 1,954 images achieved high accuracy. With the proposed framework, we have demonstrated that the combination of multi-scale structural features and synthetic data augmentation based on generative adversarial network can improve the performance of challenging tasks such as differentiating Dementia sub-types.

title: D-TINs for Track-Sampled Ice Sheet Surface Reconstruction from Satellite Altimetry Data
authors: Xiaoyu Xia, Noah Bergam, Abani Patra
abstract: Satellite altimetry samples ice sheets densely along tracks but sparsely across tracks, with frequent gaps in spatial coverage. We study the impact of this irregular support on surface reconstruction and introduce a new method, D-TIN, that applies Delaunay triangulation and barycentric interpolation directly to observed locations. A spatial holdout removes contiguous track intervals and nearby same-pass observations. We compare D-TIN with two common workflows, kriging and tile-based polynomial interpolation, to evaluate its accuracy and computational efficiency. Across seven ICESat-1 campaigns, D-TIN reduces RMSE by 12.1 m to 23.6 m relative to independent 5 km tile and polynomial based reconstruction. Its aggregate accuracy is close to the ordinary kriging workflow using a 1 km grid on the commonly used GStatSim platform while its median runtime is 252 times lower. A fixed-weight multiscale extension of D-TIN, called MS-D-TIN, gives the lowest aggregate RMSE, 67.5 m, while retaining the low computational cost of the D-TIN family.
comment: Accepted at the IEEE ICDM 2026 Workshop on Spatial and Spatiotemporal Data Mining (SSTDM 2026)

title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
authors: Jonas Motyl, Jakob S. Kottmann
abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.

title: AFNO: Universal Certifiably-Arbitrage-Free Operator Learning Framework for European Call-Price Surfaces
authors: Anastasis Kratsios, Yannick Limmer, Hans Buehler, Blanka Horvath, Raeid Saqur
abstract:
Neural operators (NOs) have been introduced as deep learning-powered solutions to the computational bottleneck of solving families of problems. Once trained, an NO can rapidly output approximate solutions, avoiding the need to rerun classical solvers. However, standard NO architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage when predicting European call-price surfaces from market or model features and, as we verify experimentally, can yield negative PnL in downstream trading tasks.
  We introduce a certifiably arbitrage-free (AF) and universal encoder-decoder NO framework, continuously mapping inputs from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $\mathcal{H}$ over any fixed subset of $[0,\infty)^2$ to a convex combination of arbitrage-free European call-price surfaces by continuously solving an approximate nearest-neighbour problem. We show that a nearest arbitrage-free correction of an unconstrained predicted surface need not exist, implying that no-arbitrage cannot, in general, be restored through post-processing. Further, we show that standard NOs, such as the FNO and certain encoder-decoder NOs, admit parameter configurations whose outputs violate static no-arbitrage. Thus, out-of-the-box NOs generally cannot be certifiably restricted to arbitrage-free configurations, but may only be guided towards them through PINN-type regularization during training.

title: Token Importance-Aware Semantic Communication Enabled Robust Video Transmission
authors: Xiwen Zhang, Yubo Peng, Luping Xiang, Kun Yang
abstract: Video applications are increasingly prevalent, yet their high data volume and temporal dependency make robust wireless transmission challenging under limited communication resources. To address this issue, we propose a token importance-aware semantic communication (Ti-SemCom) framework for bandwidth-efficient video transmission. Specifically, object and motion information is jointly extracted to identify communication-relevant regions, which are hierarchically associated with semantic tokens according to their importance. The transmitted tokens are then dynamically selected based on both token importance and the available bandwidth, prioritizing more informative video content under resource constraints. At the receiver, untransmitted regions reuse recently reconstructed references to further reduce redundant transmission. Experiments on the CAVIAR dataset show that Ti-SemCom can achieve an 88.3\% reduction in communication cost while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.

title: A constrained mixed variational formulation with Legendre-dual defects for incremental irreversible thermodynamics
authors: Mostafa Rostampour
abstract: We present a constrained mixed variational formulation for incremental irreversible thermodynamics. A single augmented action combines a linearized contact-increment penalty, equilibrium and dissipative Fenchel--Young defects, a storage--transport functional, and multipliers enforcing the constitutive increments. Under frozen-coefficient and boundary assumptions, stationarity yields the linearized contact condition, the Tisza relation, the Onsager flux--force law, and the implicit balance equation. An exact-elimination theorem shows that the contact and multiplier fields can be reconstructed algebraically from a solution of the reduced weak balance problem. We also prove off-shell invariance of the equilibrium--storage--multiplier sector under an equilibrium-sector partial Legendre transformation; invariance of the full augmented action is not claimed. For Fourier heat conduction, we derive a weighted drift identity and a per-step energy-drift bound for the energy-representation three-term incremental functional. In one spatial dimension, a small-time-step estimate yields a uniform $H^1$ bound and a discrete $L^2(0,T_f;H^2)$ bound, leading to cumulative $O(δt)$ drift over fixed time intervals. A conservative mixed discontinuous Galerkin (DG0)--Raviart--Thomas (RT0) discretization with fully implicit conductivity $κ(T)=1+T^2$ preserves discrete energy to roundoff. A separate lumped-mass piecewise-linear benchmark reproduces the predicted finite-step drift.
comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Companion paper (Part II) to be submitted

title: Is a CNN-Transformer Ensemble Worth It When a Chest X-Ray Foundation Model Is Available?
authors: Aditya Seelaboyina, Irfan Khan
abstract: Ensembles of ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks and Vision Transformers are a common way to improve multi-label chest X-ray classification. We ask whether such an ensemble is still worth its cost when a model pretrained on chest radiographs is available. On the official patient-disjoint split of NIH ChestX-ray14 (25,596 test images, 2,797 patients), we train five ImageNet-pretrained backbones and the EVA-X-S foundation model with validation-only model selection, compare five fusion rules, and estimate every difference with a patient-level paired bootstrap. EVA-X-S alone reached a test macro-AUROC of 0.828; the five-model ensemble reached 0.814 (difference -0.0136, 95% CI -0.0178 to -0.0098) at about 7.8 times the summed backbone latency and ten times the parameters. Averaging the five ImageNet models with EVA-X-S changed AUROC by -0.0056 (-0.0095 to -0.0021). With all five ImageNet backbones trained with the EVA-X-S recipe, their ensemble scored 0.817, still -0.0109 (-0.0142 to -0.0076) below EVA-X-S, and across three seeds EVA-X-S varied by at most 0.001 AUROC. Under the ImageNet models' recipe, however, EVA-X-S fell to 0.798. Our full-stacking configuration never outperformed calibrated averaging. In this setting, the tested ImageNet ensembles did not improve on a single chest X-ray foundation model fine-tuned with its own recipe.

title: Generative Learning on Manifolds for Probabilistic Seismic Performance Assessment and Structural Identifiability
authors: Dimitris G Giovanis, Ioannis G Kevrekidis, Roger G Ghanem
abstract: Seismic performance assessment relies on computationally expensive nonlinear simulations, limiting uncertainty quantification and inference of structural properties from observed responses. We develop a manifold-based generative framework that learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and seismic-response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations. Combining Diffusion Maps, score-based Diffusion Modeling, and Geometric Harmonics, the framework enables both forward probabilistic prediction and inverse inference. Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the results reveal which structural properties are identifiable from seismic performance and how uncertainty in these properties influences response. In particular, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation characteristics more effectively than individual strength parameters. Inverse inference identifies distinct structural configurations that produce similar seismic performance, with representative solutions independently validated using nonlinear simulations. These findings demonstrate how generative learning can support uncertainty-aware seismic assessment while revealing structural non-identifiability and alternative mechanisms underlying observed performance

title: Artifact Filtering versus Artifact-Compensated Training in JPEG to JPEG AI Recompression
authors: Igor Podtsepko, Yuriy Kim, Karam Mahfod, Evgeny Belyaev, Kristian Kirs, Jianping Lin, Ilya Papiev
abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of recompression of images from JPEG to JPEG AI format. We show that direct recompression from JPEG to JPEG~AI trained on uncompressed images is accompanied by the preservation of the JPEG image artifacts in the resulting JPEG~AI image. In order to avoid it, we evaluate an approach where an artifacts removal neural network is first applied to the input JPEG image as an external pre-filter. However, in this case, the processing time is increased by 29 times. Therefore, we propose an artifact-compensated training for JPEG AI and show that it is able to combine pre-filtering against target distortions with efficient compression without increase in the processing time.
comment: Preprint. Submitted to IEEE Multimedia on 21 February 2026. This is the author's draft version; it has not undergone peer review. 15 pages, 8 figures

title: On the Concavity of Rényi Entropy and Rényi Entropy Power along Heat Flows on Manifolds
authors: Hao Wu, Lei Yu
abstract: In this paper, we establish the concavity of Rényi entropy and Rényi entropy power along heat flow on Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension, for Rényi orders $α\in[1,2]$. More generally, we prove the corresponding result along the heat flow generated by the Witten Laplacian on complete Riemannian manifolds under a suitable curvature-dimension condition. Our argument builds on novel functional inequalities that were recently developed for the study of Tsallis entropy concavity along the heat flow. We extend both these inequalities and the resulting concavity theorem from the Euclidean setting to the Riemannian manifold setting. In addition, we establish the complete monotonicity of Tsallis entropy of order $2$ along the heat flow and derive its spectral decomposition.

title: Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs for Solving the 3D Stokes Equations on Unstructured Meshes: Novel Techniques and Advances
authors: Farjana Siddiqua, Haoxiang Huang, Weiming Ding, Haotian Sun, Vigor Yang, Yingjie Liu
abstract: Neural-network surrogates for fluid-flow PDEs usually learn the solution globally, which requires large networks and many high-fidelity training simulations. Neural networks with local converging inputs (NNLCI) instead work locally. They predict the high-fidelity solution at a point from two converging coarse-grid solutions sampled near that point, which keeps the network small, needs little training data, and generalizes across geometries. Here, the two low-fidelity meshes, LF1 and LF2, have on average about 300 and 730 tetrahedra, compared with about 155,000 in the high-fidelity mesh (HF). In this work, we develop an NNLCI framework for three-dimensional Stokes equations on unstructured tetrahedral meshes and introduce two techniques for building local inputs near complex curved boundaries. First, input patches may extend beyond the boundary, with the outside values obtained from a local least-squares fit, so that every high-fidelity point can be predicted, including those next to the wall. Second, the local mesh spacing is estimated from neighboring centroids, which sets the stencil size consistently on unstructured meshes. For pipe flows with one to three bumps, including a circumferentially rotated bump, NNLCI reduces the relative $L^2$ error of the finer low-fidelity solution by $90\%$ to $94\%$, evaluated at all high-fidelity points. Both techniques carry over to other NNLCI problems with smooth solutions on point-cloud discretizations.

title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
authors: Lluís Arola-Fernández, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Supplemental Material included (10 pages). Code: https://github.com/mystic-blue/radiohead

title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
authors: Konstantinos Karagiannis
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code, data, IBM Quantum shot records, transpiled circuits and calibration snapshots in ancillary files. Prepared with AI assistance; see "Use of AI tools"

title: Autonomous Optimization of Numerical Algorithms by an AI Agent: Application to Atomistic Simulation
authors: Jeheon Woo
abstract: Coding agents built on large language models, run in automated improvement loops, can discover more efficient algorithms. We present AIOA, a framework that brings this approach to the numerical algorithms of atomistic simulation: an agent improves an algorithm against a pre-specified metric in a loop guarded by verifiers it cannot alter. Applied to ASE, a widely used atomistic simulation library, AIOA targets two facets of an algorithm: its implementation, rewritten to run faster with unchanged results, and the method itself, redesigned to converge with fewer force evaluations. Agents made six kernels 22-24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy. On unseen problems, optimizers from the best configuration needed 3.1-3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6-17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths. The agents' optimizers also contain two algorithmic components we did not find in the literature.
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information included

title: RALES: A Risk-Averse Augmented Lagrangian Equality-Constrained SQP Method
authors: Harbir Antil, Drew P. Kouri, Denis Ridzal, Thomas M. Surowiec
abstract: This paper develops RALES, an augmented Lagrangian method for risk-averse optimization in function spaces with nonsmooth risk measures, nonlinear equality constraints, and convex geometric constraints. The method combines safeguarded risk and constraint multiplier updates with efficient sequential quadratic programming based on inexact subproblem solves. The analysis establishes asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems and gives conditions for feasibility of weak primal accumulation points. Under additional assumptions on subproblem accuracy, duality, and boundedness, it provides global primal optimality guarantees and weak convergence of the full stored and candidate multiplier sequences to a common dual maximizer. Dual convergence is strong when all penalty parameters remain bounded. Numerical experiments for a finitely sampled semilinear PDE control problem, with the Conditional Value-at-Risk and the Mean-Plus-Semideviation risk measures, illustrate the method's performance as the spatial mesh is refined and as the number of samples increases.

title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
authors: Shai Ben-David, Steve Hanneke, Farnam Mansouri, Amirreza Shaeiri
abstract: We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.

title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
authors: Wei Wang, Po-Yu Liang, Jun Bai
abstract: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.

title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
authors: Malcolm Wolff, Elliott Zackrone, Souhaib Ben Taieb, Michael W. Mahoney, Kin G. Olivares
abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.
comment: International Journal of Forecasting (Work in progress paper)

title: Unilluminable rooms: minimal examples, classifications and exceptions
authors: J. C. F. de Winter, George W. Tokarsky
abstract: A room with mirrored walls can contain two points that are mutually invisible: no light ray from one reaches the other. Tokarsky built the first polygonal examples by tiling a room with reflected copies of a triangle and making every tile vertex of certain kinds a corner of the room. We study the smallest rooms of this kind, which we call lattice rooms. Their interior tile vertices of the remaining kind, the sources, are invisible and pairwise mutually invisible. On the tiling by isosceles right triangles, a hole-free lattice room with a source has at least 12 sides, attained only by the pinwheel. On the square tiling the least number is 16, again attained by one room. A hole-free lattice room with two sources has at least 24 sides on the first tiling and 34 on the square tiling. Up to congruence there are 12 such rooms with 24 sides, 89 with 25 sides and 14 with 34 sides. One absorbing post, one partition, or one hole that touches the outer boundary at one point lowers the least number of sides for two sources to 18, 20 and 22 (21 if sides are counted as maximal straight segments). Two and three posts give 17 and 16 sides, and a hole that does not touch the outer boundary gives 26. We list all smallest rooms. Rooms assembled from n modules have exactly 12n sides and n sources, and a hole-free lattice room with three or more sources has at least 36 sides. We also give rooms in which some tile vertices need not be corners: 15 types of 27-sided rooms on the tiling by triangles with angles 30, 60 and 90 degrees, which are smallest in their class, a nonagon with three mutually invisible corners, and a 42-sided room in which a rotation through 180 degrees takes the place of a corner. In a ring of three trapezoids a light ray returns to a corner that is invisible in one trapezoid. Several classifications rely on exhaustive computer searches made finite by the bounds proved here.
comment: 36 pages, 19 figures. Programs and data are included as ancillary files

title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
authors: David Gill, Victoria Prowse, J. Lucas Reddinger
abstract: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.
comment: 90 pages, including appendices. JEL: C73, C92, D91, J24

title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
authors: David Gill, Zhongheng Qiao
abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.
comment: 71 pages, including appendices. JEL: C91, D03, D83, D91, J24

title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
authors: Shi Bo, Jiaming Hu
abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.

title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
authors: Olga Isupova, Danil Kuzin, Fredrik Gustafsson, Lyudmila Mihaylova
abstract: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.

title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
authors: Albert Shaju, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Mingzhe Chen
abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.
comment: 6 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027

title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
authors: Sawyer Dobson, Zhenghan Wang
abstract: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
authors: Gokul Bhusal, Delanna Do, Ekaterina Merkurjev, Kevin Miller, Stephan Wojtowytsch
abstract: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

title: MRFoundry: Knowledge-guided agent loops for end-to-end MRI research
authors: Ke Wang, Atakan Topcu, Hossein Momeni, Molin Zhang
abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.
comment: 18 pages, including 6 pages of Supporting Information. Code: https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry

title: A probabilistic model of visual segmentation explains early visual cortical dynamics
authors: Tridib K. Biswas, Ruben Coen-Cagli
abstract: Neural dynamics are a central feature of biological neural systems. In the visual cortex, the functional role of neural dynamics is poorly understood, particularly for static stimuli. The statistics of still natural images have long been used by models that successfully predict firing in early visual cortex; those models assume that neurons represent inferences about latent image features, but often ignore the dynamics of said inference. Here, we test if inferential dynamics in images explain visual-cortical dynamics. To do so, we present a biologically plausible model of cortical computation which assumes that the inference of features is coupled with inference about how those features are organized into meaningful parts, a function also known as segmentation. Given an input image, our model iterates between inferring the features and the segments, through recurrence and feedback, thus inducing dynamics in the neural representation of features. For these neural dynamics, we derive theoretical and exact predictions. Our model predicts both gain and variability in evoked responses to natural images, and we show that it captures classical single-neuron experimental findings such as gain dynamics and variability decay during stimulus presentation. The model also predicts that those dynamics are organized around inferred segment structure and more heterogeneous than previously thought, reflecting the complexity of inference for natural scenes. Finally, our analytical formulation provides a clear interpretation of our results. Insights from our normative model could generalize to segmentation problems in other experimental modalities, and help address the cost of inference in artificial networks with iterative computation.
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
authors: Maria Franz, N. Benjamin Erichson
abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the AI4DD workshop (AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap), NeurIPS 2026

title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
authors: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

title: Off-target posterior mass: A training-free diagnostic for fine-tuning spoken language diarization probes
authors: Zhuoyan Tao, Aditya Kommineni, Shrikanth Narayanan
abstract: Spoken Language Diarization (SLD) models provide frame-level language information of a speech recording. SLD modeling pipeline includes feature extraction from pre-trained speech models followed by clustering. Fine-tuning pre-trained speech models has shown performance gains for SLD with its magnitude being dataset dependent. Off-target Posterior Mass (OTPM), computed based on posterior language identification probabilities is proposed as a diagnostic metric to forecast performance gains from SLD fine-tuning. OTPM obtains positive correlation with probe gains, 0.56 on unseen synthetic bilingual data and 0.23 on real-world corpora. These results indicate promising potential of OTPM as a diagnostic metric for SLD.
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to JASA Express Letters

title: Orthographic depth at two scales, with English also matched for lexicon size
authors: Adam Y. Shavit
abstract: A reader can struggle to read in only one of their languages, and one proposed reason is how predictably spelling maps to sound. We measure that predictability as conditional entropy, the pronunciation uncertainty left once the spelling is seen, at two grain sizes (unit sizes): the alignment unit, an aligned spelling-sound chunk, and the syllable, bounded in the pronunciation. We analyse word lists in twelve alphabetic orthographies and report five in full, with English pronunciations from a dictionary and the rest from the synthesizer eSpeak-ng, length marks removed. Among the five, English has the most uncertainty and Finnish the least at both grains. Across all twelve, Portuguese and Danish exceed English per alignment unit, and German and Italian order differently by grain and transcription. These orders hold when English is transcribed by eSpeak-ng with u allowed to spell /j/ plus a vowel. Uncertainty per unit has no shared direction as units grow: it falls in Spanish and, less securely, German, is level in Finnish, depends on transcription in Italian and on the word list in English, and rises in Norwegian and Swedish. Summed uncertainty per word falls in all twelve, but that score is handed the pronunciation's boundaries and mixes context with in-sample memorisation, so it is no evidence of what a reader computes. An exact identity states when discarded spelling boundaries could reverse that fall. A uniform 20,000-word English sample holds 35% of the dictionary's syllable spellings and has syllable entropy 0.098 bits lower, so lexicons must be matched in size. In an exploratory check over eleven languages, syllable-scale entropy tracked first-year reading accuracy (rho = -0.74, falling to -0.25 if English is given the lowest entropy instead), without separating the syllable scale from the alignment unit. These estimates describe sampled writing systems, not readers.
comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Spelling-to-sound entropy as a measure of orthographic depth for cross-language reading research; exploratory check against Grade 1 reading accuracy in Section 3.5. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A9T3C

title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
authors: Xintao Xia, Jia Gu
abstract: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.

title: Complete Decentralization of Wave Equation Control on a Compact Domain
authors: Addie McCurdy, Emily Jensen
abstract: A feedback control policy is completely decentralized if the actuation signal at each location in space can be computed based only on state information from that location. For systems equipped with large numbers of spatially distributed sensors and actuators, completely decentralized controllers are desirable since they can be implemented in a communication and computation efficient manner, but generally perform worse than centralized counterparts. However, through a case study of Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) design for wave dynamics on a compact spatial domain, we show that careful design of system parameters to satisfy certain conditions causes a decentralized control policy to perform as well as any centralized policy. We then propose a spatially filtered $H_2$ norm to show that satisfying these conditions does not inherently degrade achievable closed-loop system performance, enabling simultaneous realization of both desirable performance and communication/computation efficiency via system-control co-design. Additional robustness analysis characterizes a range of system parameters such that the system interconnected with a decentralized controller maintains stability and near-optimal performance. Although our framework is derived for spatially continuous dynamics, we demonstrate that this theory can be leveraged to derive results for decentralization in finite-dimensional settings through a damped mass-spring example.
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, submitted to SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization

title: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
authors: Yilin Zheng, Haowei Wang, Wenjia Wang, Szu Hui Ng
abstract: Simulation optimization typically returns a single estimated optimal point. When decisions also depend on criteria evaluated independently of simulation, such as resource cost, the decision maker instead needs the set of designs whose expected performance lies within a tolerance of the optimum, often choosing the tolerance only after seeing the tradeoffs. We study how to identify these near-optimal regions on a continuous design space, simultaneously for all tolerances up to a prescribed maximum $T$, with region estimation error at most $η$. We show that region identification is not a by-product of optimization. Specifically, when $α>ν$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $Ω\bigl(η^{-(2+d/ν)}\min\{1,KT^{d/α}\}\bigr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $ν$ the smoothness, and $(K,α)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. We propose SASORI, which returns an estimated optimal point and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching this lower bound up to logarithmic factors. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

title: Statistical Analysis of the Structure from Noise Phenomenon in Generalized Procrustes Problems
authors: Jiayang Yin, Shuyang Ling
abstract: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), observations are highly noisy, and scientists often use reference templates to guide matching, alignment, and averaging to reconstruct the molecular structure. However, these procedures can produce an output resembling the template even when the observations contain only noise, a phenomenon known as Einstein from noise (EfN). This phenomenon has attracted attention in statistics, where simplified observation models involving group actions have been studied to understand the resulting model bias. Characterizing the bias in the full cryo-EM pipeline remains challenging. We study template matching and averaging in the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem, which provides an analytically tractable setting involving continuous orthogonal group action and lower-dimensional projections of ordered point clouds. We show that, for pure Gaussian noise, the mean of the aligned-and-averaged estimator admits the same left and right singular-vector bases as the template but its singular values may be distorted. This identifies the subspace structure imposed by the template even in the absence of signal. We characterize the singular values and bound their distortion, establish finite-sample operator-norm bounds, and give sufficient sample sizes for the population mean to dominate random fluctuations. In fact, this bias still exists under weak signals: when the template rank is at least the observation dimension, the change from the pure-noise mean is $O(η^2)$ in signal amplitude $η$. Our results provide an explicit characterization of model bias in a registration problem motivated by cryo-EM and show why averaging more observations can stabilize structure imposed by the template without removing the bias.

title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
authors: Daniel Barter, Jacob C. Bridgeman, Chris Dawson, Terry Farrelly, Shane Fleming, Mercedes Gimeno-Segovia, Paul Hartke, Timothy Hein, Sean Howell, Gregory Hyegang Jun, Siddhartha Kamalakara, Yehua Liu, Jose M. Monsalve Diaz, Eddie Richter, Sam Roberts
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

title: Toward Pseudorange-Based PNT with Starlink: A Mock Fused LEO GNSS Implementation
authors: Samuel C. Morgan, Zacharias M. Komodromos, Wenkai Qin, Andrew Graff, Zachary L. Clements, W. Jeremy Morrison, Todd E. Humphreys
abstract:
We present experimental results from Starlink for pseudorange-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), emulating a system that fuses a primary communications mission with a secondary low-Earth orbit (LEO) PNT mission. Legacy global navigation satellite system (GNSS) constellations faceinherent vulnerabilities and signal limitations, prompting growing interest in
  broadband LEO constellations---such as SpaceX's Starlink---for resilient PNT. However, opportunistic use of stand-alone Starlink signals fails to achieve
  GNSS-competitive accuracy due to frame timing irregularities and reliance on uncorrected poor-quality publicly available ephemeris data. To overcome these limitations, we present a mock
  implementation of a fused LEO GNSS architecture. Our method extracts time-of-arrival observables from live Starlink Ku-band downlinks and pairs them with high-fidelity, beam-specific orbit and clock models distributed as if provided natively by the constellation operator. In a field campaign, and despite constraints imposed by consumer-grade receiver hardware, the method
  yields 95% error bounds of 2.33 m horizontally (semi-major axis), 3.37 m vertically, and 11.19 ns in timing, with the actual solution errors falling well within these bounds.

title: Emilia2: A Large-Scale Dataset for Controllable Long-Form Speech Generation
authors: Qinke Ni, Dekun Chen, Junwen Qiu, Huan Liao, Xu Li, Xingwen Han, Wan Lin, Kunyu Feng, Yuxiang Wang, Yusheng Mu, Chaoren Wang, Yingda Shen, Mingjie Chen, Haolong Zheng, Xulin Fan, Mark A. Hasegawa-Johnson, Zhizheng Wu
abstract: Generating long-form speech requires models to keep content, speaker identity, turn-taking, and expressive style consistent over time. Yet most open training corpora contain examples lasting only tens of seconds and open long-form benchmarks cover at most two speakers per recording. We introduce Emilia2, a 229K-hour multilingual dataset for controllable long-form speech generation. From in-the-wild data, Emilia2 constructs short utterances, single-speaker long-form speech, and multi-speaker dialogues, preserving transcripts, speaker identities, pauses, and acoustic transitions. Examples longer than five minutes account for 50.0% of single-speaker long-form hours and 66.8% of dialogue hours. To support expressive control, Emilia2 provides natural language instructions for 4.77M examples and nonverbal-vocalization tags for 933K examples. We also introduce Emilia2-testset, 23 hours of bilingual recordings of up to 30 minutes and four speakers, each speaker paired with reference audio. We train autoregressive (AR) and non-autoregressive (NAR) models on Emilia2. Our 0.6B-backbone NAR model achieves the lowest Chinese CER and English WER on TTSD-Eval (5.27%/9.93%) among compared systems, while our AR model is on par with Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-VD on InstructTTSEval (zh/en: 76.2/78.3 vs. 77.1/77.9). These results validate Emilia2 as a comprehensive data foundation for long-form speech generation and minute-scale expressive control. Demo: https://charlesnii.github.io/Emilia2-demo/.
zh_title: Emilia2：一个用于可控长语音生成的大规模数据集
translation: 生成长篇语音需要模型随时间推移保持内容、说话人身份、轮流对话以及表达风格的一致性。然而，大多数开放训练语料库只包含持续数十秒的样本，开放的长语音基准测试每个录音最多涵盖两个说话人。我们介绍了 Emilia2，这是一个包含 229K 小时的多语言数据集，用于可控长语音生成。从野外数据中，Emilia2 构建了短话语、单人长语音和多人对话，保留了转录本、说话人身份、停顿和声学转换。超过五分钟的样本占单人长语音小时数的 50.0% 和对话小时数的 66.8%。为了支持表达控制，Emilia2 为 477 万个样本提供了自然语言指令，为 93 万个样本提供了非言语发声标签。我们还推出了 Emilia2-testset，这是一个包含长达 30 分钟、最多 4 个说话人的双语录音测试集，共 23 小时，每个说话人都配有参考音频。我们在 Emilia2 上训练了自回归（AR）和非自回归（NAR）模型。我们的 0.6B 骨干 NAR 模型在 TTSD-Eval 上实现了对比系统中最低的中文 CER 和英文 WER（5.27%/9.93%），而我们的 AR 模型在 InstructTTSEval 上的表现与 Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-VD 相当（zh/en: 76.2/78.3 对比 77.1/77.9）。这些结果验证了 Emilia2 作为长语音生成和分钟级表达控制的全面数据基础。演示地址：https://charlesnii.github.io/Emilia2-demo/。
tldr: Emilia2是一个229K小时的多语言长语音生成数据集，通过提供丰富的长时音频和控制标签，显著提升了语音合成模型的长时一致性和表达控制能力。
ai_comments: Emilia2通过构建大规模、多语言、长时序的语音数据集，有效解决了目前开源长语音数据和基准测试严重不足的问题，对可控长语音生成领域具有重要的推动作用。
motivation: 现有的公开训练语料多为数十秒的短音频，且开源长语音基准测试每个录音最多涵盖两名说话人，无法满足可控长语音生成的需求。
method: 从野外数据中构建短语料、单人长语音以及多人对话，并提供自然语言指令和非语言发音标签，同时训练了自回归（AR）和非自回归（NAR）模型。
results: 基于Emilia2训练的0.6B骨干NAR模型在TTSD-Eval上取得了最低的中文CER和英文WER，AR模型在InstructTTSEval上的表现也与Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-VD相当。
conclusion: Emilia2是一个全面且高质量的长语音生成数据基础，有效提升了自回归和非自回归模型在长语音生成和表达控制方面的性能。

title: Exact (Non-)Accelerations of Heavy-Ball Discretizations
authors: Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Takáč
abstract: Momentum methods with the same slow dynamics can have different worst-case rates on smooth strongly convex functions. We identify a half-step phase barrier in the gradient query that governs this difference. For momentum with extrapolation $τ_κ\toτ$, $β=1-θ/\sqrtκ+o(κ^{-1/2})$ and $hL\to y$, where $κ=L/μ$ and $θ,y>0$, the exact uniform distance factor is $1-c/\sqrtκ+o(κ^{-1/2})$, with $c=\min\{θ/3,c_Q(θ,y)\}$, when $τ>1/2$ and $y(1+2τ)<4$; $c_Q$ is the slowest quadratic decay exponent. Quadratically accelerated families with $\limsupτ_κ<1/2$ have divergent trajectories on the full function class. Upper bounds use finite-lag certificates: nonnegative combinations of inequalities for values and gradients at finitely separated query points, together with comparisons to the minimizer. For any prescribed accuracy, spiral mixtures or quadratic trajectories of one finite-dimensional objective give matching lower bounds at all iteration horizons. We resolve the parameter layer near $τ=1/2$ and classify all tunings of this family attaining the optimal leading constant 1. The flow also bounds the leading constant of every second-order stationary linear family with the same slow parameters $(θ,y)$ and fixed finite memory.
comment: 63 pages, 7 figures, link to Lean formalization
zh_title: 重球离散化的精确（非）加速
translation: 具有相同慢动力学的动量方法在光滑强凸函数上可能具有不同的最坏情况速率。我们确定了梯度查询中的一个半步相屏障，它控制着这种差异。对于外推 $τ_κ	oτ$, $β=1-θ/\sqrtκ+o(κ^{-1/2})$ 和 $hL	o y$ 的动量方法，其中 $κ=L/μ$ 且 $θ,y>0$，当 $τ>1/2$ 且 $y(1+2τ)<4$ 时，精确的统一距离因子是 $1-c/\sqrtκ+o(κ^{-1/2})$，其中 $c=\min\{θ/3,c_Q(θ,y)\}$；$c_Q$ 是最慢的二次衰减指数。二次加速族，其 $\limsupτ_κ<1/2$，在完整的函数类上具有发散轨迹。上限使用有限滞后证书：在有限分离查询点处的值和梯度的不等式的非负组合，以及与最小值的比较。对于任何预设精度，一个有限维目标的螺旋混合或二次轨迹在所有迭代范围内提供匹配的下限。我们解决了 $τ=1/2$ 附近的参数层，并分类了该家族所有达到最优主导常数 1 的调整。该流还限制了所有具有相同慢参数 $(θ,y)$ 和固定有限记忆的二阶平稳线性家族的主导常数。
tldr: 本文揭示了具有相同慢动力学的动量方法在光滑强凸函数上具有不同最坏情况收敛速率的原因，确定了梯度查询中的半步相屏障是关键因素，并给出了精确的统一距离因子，解决了τ=1/2附近的参数层问题，并对达到最优常数的调整进行了分类。
ai_comments: 本文对动量方法的收敛行为进行了深刻的理论分析，特别是揭示了导致不同最坏情况速率的细微差异。识别“半步相屏障”并推导出精确的统一距离因子是重要的创新。解决τ=1/2附近的参数层和分类最优调整为算法设计提供了实用的见解。其将发现推广到一般的二阶平稳线性家族，表明了其广泛的适用性。使用有限滞后证书和特定目标轨迹进行界限分析展示了严谨的数学方法。
motivation: 具有相同慢动力学的动量方法在光滑强凸函数上可能具有不同的最坏情况速率，这促使研究人员探索并解释这种差异的根源。
method: 本文通过识别梯度查询中的半步相屏障来分析动量方法，并使用有限滞后证书（finite-lag certificates）结合值和梯度的不等式以及与最小值的比较来建立上限。对于下限，则使用螺旋混合或一个有限维目标的二次轨迹。研究还包括对τ=1/2附近参数层的解析和对最优调整的分类。
results: 研究发现，梯度查询中的半步相屏障控制着动量方法最坏情况速率的差异。当τ>1/2且y(1+2τ)<4时，精确的统一距离因子为1-c/√κ+o(κ^(-1/2))，其中c=min{θ/3,c_Q(θ,y)}。limsupτ_κ<1/2的二次加速族在完整的函数类上具有发散轨迹。论文解决了τ=1/2附近的参数层问题，并分类了所有达到最优主导常数1的调整。该流还限制了所有具有相同慢参数(θ,y)和固定有限记忆的二阶平稳线性家族的主导常数。
conclusion: 本文确定了导致动量方法不同最坏情况收敛速率的关键因素——梯度查询中的半步相屏障，并提供了精确的收敛速率分析。它解决了关键的参数区域，分类了最优的算法调整，并将其发现扩展到更广泛的二阶线性家族，为动量算法的设计和理解提供了深入的理论基础。
